tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_scrape
tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state. `firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call. Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. # reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Applications: The Strain of Success (SSAC24)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Weekly game-week planning for football position groups. The talk's core move is scoring each player on two numbers before each match (a skill rating and a next-match injury probability) and then deciding who plays. Applied Performance could build a simple version for one group (for example defensive backs or running backs), pairing the player's PFF-based grade with a workload-and-history risk flag, and bring it to coaches as a rest-or-play conversation, not a verdict.
- Inference: Choosing which workload features to put in front of coaches. The speaker reported that short-term and long-term workload and detailed injury history contributed most to the injury model, with travel, rain, temperature and age contributing less [04:33]. For Baylor, that points toward trusting Catapult load history and Athletic Medicine injury history over contextual variables when deciding what to track.
- Inference: The "greedy versus lookahead" framing is a useful lens on in-season decisions. The speaker said real managers behave closer to a greedy, match-by-match approach [10:12], and the Q&A suggested re-optimizing over a short window instead of the whole season [16:20]. A Baylor version is a bye-week and late-season plan: which players get reduced exposure in lower-leverage games.
- Inference: Retrospective audit as a low-risk use. Replay last season's depth chart decisions against Catapult load and injury dates to see where heavy repeated workload preceded soft-tissue injuries, without changing any live decision.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, through sound load progression and collaboration with Athletic Medicine (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk agrees in spirit: the speaker said it is a decision framework, not an expert medical prediction model [18:54], and claimed reduced injury incidence, not prevention.
- Eric's baseline: abrupt changes in volume or intensity are treated as an injury-risk driver, and recovery has to be earned by training hard first (course team positions). The talk extends the first point (workload history is the top feature [04:33]) but sits in tension with the second: its premise is resting players more at chosen moments, and the baseline warns that load-monitoring culture drifted toward under-training.
- Eric's baseline: no formal injury-risk model is attributed to Eric in the corpus, and ACWR-style modeling there is reference material only. The talk therefore adds something Eric has no stated position on, and any adoption would be new method, not confirmation.
- Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost versus insight, and a valid test can still be wrong operationally without consistent collection. The talk's own limit (public data only, no GPS or medical data [13:48]) is the reverse of Baylor's situation, where the inputs exist but would need to be consistently clean.

## What would have to be true

- Several seasons of consistent Catapult data per athlete, linked to Athletic Medicine injury records with dates and durations, so a Baylor injury model could be trained and checked on its own data.
- Enough injuries per position group to fit anything stable. Inference: with a roster this size and soft-tissue injuries this infrequent, one group may be too few events, so pooling groups or seasons would be required.
- A skill value per player that coaches accept (the talk used a player contribution model, caption spelling "VAPE" [05:36]); at Baylor that would be PFF grades or a coach-approved ranking.
- Coaches willing to treat the output as one input. The Q&A noted that a team has to be convinced to make decisions on it [18:54].

## Do not apply when

- Inference: The model assumes a weekly schedule of roughly 38 or 39 league matches [15:19] and full-match rest decisions only [13:48]. A 12-game football season with a full-game rest option has far fewer decisions to optimize, and football uses rotation and snap counts more than all-or-nothing starts.
- The talk's results come from simulation on open Premier League data and an imputed workload model [17:53]. The speaker said the injury model was not the main focus. Do not treat the 13% or 11% figures as expected Baylor effects.
- Inference: Collision-sport injury mechanisms differ from soccer. The speaker only tested higher injury-risk multipliers as a stand-in for rugby or American football [11:44] and listed real testing there as future work [14:18].
- Resting a starter in a college game carries eligibility, scholarship and recruiting considerations the model does not represent.

## First step

Pick one position group and one past season. In a spreadsheet, list each player's weekly Catapult player load, game snaps and any Athletic Medicine soft-tissue injury dates, and mark the weeks with the highest rolling load before each injury. Look at it with Athletic Medicine only; make no change to live decisions.

# Applications: Have the Nerds Ruined Basketball? (SSAC25)

## Where this applies

- Inference: Weighting what athletes and coaches say against what they do. One panelist described giving stated survey data limited weight next to behavioral data such as minute-by-minute viewing [14:50], and described lab studies using heart rate and skin temperature monitors [15:20]. For Baylor, this supports treating athlete-reported or coach-reported readiness as one input beside force plate and GPS measures.
- Inference: Watching for a narrative that outruns the evidence. A panelist argued that a media story about three-pointers shaped fan attitudes without evidence that the story was true [12:19]. In football analytics, a similar risk is a single popular metric (a PFF grade, a load number) becoming shorthand in staff conversations before anyone has checked what it predicts.
- Inference: Spotting convergence when every program optimizes the same lever. Daryl (caption spelling) argued that teams all push toward what the rules reward [22:29]. For recruiting grading, check whether a grade built on public data leads to the same targets as every other program, and whether Baylor's edge sits in non-public inputs.
- Inference: Intern and analyst development. The hiring exercise asked panelists to split 100 points across analytical ability, interpersonal skills and passion [35:05], with answers such as 40, 40 and 20 [36:06]. This can be a prompt for what Applied Performance should look for when selecting interns.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes learned to game them, replaced by objective mRSI from force plates, and kept only for return-to-play and chronic-condition cases. The talk agrees: its panelists put behavioral data ahead of stated preferences [14:50], though that was about fans, not athletes.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters at least as much as technology for daily assessment (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk partly conflicts with a pure objective-first view and partly agrees: one panelist said fans do not realize how hard players' plays are [14:20], which is a case for expert observation over lay reports.
- Eric's baseline: interns need both the "why" and the "how," plus a portfolio of real work products. The hiring exercise is consistent with weighting more than analytical skill, but the speakers did not describe training design.
- No direct link found to the rule-change, three-point or fan-engagement content.

## What would have to be true

- Before applying the "behavior over stated preference" idea, Baylor needs behavioral data that is consistently collected (force plate trends, GPS load, attendance at optional sessions), not just the survey.
- To judge convergence in recruiting, a comparison against other programs' grades or draft and portfolio outcomes, which the talk did not supply.
- For the hiring exercise, agreement among Applied Performance staff on what each category means for the specific job.

## Do not apply when

- The panel is basketball league-office and team executives debating entertainment value and rule design. Inference: Football rule changes and fan preference are outside Applied Performance's control, so none of the rule-change content transfers to practice decisions.
- Several figures are garbled in the captions, such as the variance of play styles between teams [10:47] and the three-point attempt questions [38:40]. Do not cite them.
- The panelists speak from institutional positions (NBA league office, a team, the 76ers). Treat their statements about fans as the speakers' own views, not evidence about Baylor athletes or fans.
- Inference: Fan-weighting scores (3, 5, 6 to 7 [14:50]) were offered casually in a panel setting and say nothing about how to weight athlete feedback.

## First step

Take the last term's athlete-reported readiness or soreness entries, if any, and compare them with that week's force plate or GPS values for the same athletes in a spreadsheet. See whether the two move together. Share with the staff as a discussion item only; no change to monitoring practice.

For recruiting grading, check whether a grade built on public data leads to the same targets as every other program, and whether Baylor's edge sits in non-public inputs.
- Inference: Intern and analyst development. The hiring exercise asked panelists to split 100 points across analytical ability, interpersonal skills and passion [35:05], with answers such as 40, 40 and 20 [36:06]. This can be a prompt for what Applied Performance should look for when selecting interns.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys were dropped for general roster use because athletes learned to game them, replaced by objective mRSI from force plates, and kept only for return-to-play and chronic-condition cases. The talk agrees: its panelists put behavioral data ahead of stated preferences [14:50], though that was about fans, not athletes.
- Eric's baseline: a trained coach's eye matters at least as much as technology for daily assessment (course team position, speaker unconfirmed). The talk partly conflicts with a pure objective-first view and partly agrees: one panelist said fans do not realize how hard players' plays are [14:20], which is a case for expert observation over lay reports.
- Eric's baseline: interns need both the "why" and the "how," plus a portfolio of real work products. The hiring exercise is consistent with weighting more than analytical skill, but the speakers did not describe training design.
- No direct link found to the rule-change, three-point or fan-engagement content.

## What would have to be true

- Before applying the "behavior over stated preference" idea, Baylor needs behavioral data that is consistently collected (force plate trends, GPS load, attendance at optional sessions), not just the survey.
- To judge convergence in recruiting, a comparison against other programs' grades or draft and portfolio outcomes, which the talk did not supply.
- For the hiring exercise, agreement among Applied Performance staff on what each category means for the specific job.

## Do not apply when

- The panel is basketball league-office and team executives debating entertainment value and rule design. Inference: Football rule changes and fan preference are outside Applied Performance's control, so none of the rule-change content transfers to practice decisions.
- Several figures are garbled in the captions, such as the variance of play styles between teams [10:47] and the three-point attempt questions [38:40]. Do not cite them.
- The panelists speak from institutional positions (NBA league office, a team, the 76ers). Treat their statements about fans as the speakers' own views, not evidence about Baylor athletes or fans.
- Inference: Fan-weighting scores (3, 5, 6 to 7 [14:50]) were offered casually in a panel setting and say nothing about how to weight athlete feedback.

## First step

Take the last term's athlete-reported readiness or soreness entries, if any, and compare them with that week's force plate or GPS values for the same athletes in a spreadsheet. See whether the two move together. Share with the staff as a discussion item only; no change to monitoring practice.

=== FILE: videos/2024-03-20_K5a7C4b1Cwc_the-strain-of-success-a-predictive-model-for-injury-mitigati/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: K5a7C4b1Cwc
title: "SSAC24: The Strain of Success: A Predictive Model for Injury Mitigation and Team Success in Soccer"
event: SSAC24 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Ryan Beiel (caption spelling), Greg Everett (lead author, appears in recorded segments)]
topics: [sports-science, injury-health, decision-making, other-sport:soccer]
confidence: supported
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

The presenters propose a team-selection model for soccer that tries to cut injuries without giving up points. Each player gets a skill rating and a next-match injury probability. A Monte Carlo tree search then simulates the coming weeks to choose the starting eleven, treating the coach's job as a sequential decision problem. Tested on open Premier League data against a greedy pick-the-best-team-each-week baseline, the model reduced simulated injuries while keeping expected points similar, and the speakers argue real managers lean toward short-term choices. They state the work is a decision framework built on public data, not a clinical prediction tool.

## Key claims

- The work was motivated by crowded schedules; after the winter World Cup, injury severity rose and injury costs reached very large figures [01:01].
- Each player has a skill rating and an injury probability, and a search over team selections balances winning now against injury risk later [02:01].
- Resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, but the coach has to pick the right moment [03:02].
- Short-term and long-term workload and detailed injury history contributed most to the injury model, ahead of travel, rain, days since last injury, temperature and age [04:33].
- The team-level scoring model was modified to use player skill values and matched the original model within margins of error over two seasons [06:06].
- Compared with a greedy selection, the search model kept similar expected points while lowering injuries for the squad and the ideal starting eleven [11:14].
- Real managers' selections were more similar to the greedy model than to the search model; the speakers suggest short-term pressure as the reason [10:43].
- In higher injury-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy one on season points, while the margin of injury reduction shrank [12:15].
- Real technical directors often decide for short-term gains rather than long-term athlete protection [14:48].
- The presenters conclude teams can rest athletes and reduce injury risk without sacrificing results [14:48].

## Numbers and definitions

- 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup [01:01].
- Almost $770 million in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season [01:01]. The Q&A-adjacent conclusion later says "nearly $800 million" [12:46]; the two spoken figures differ and the captions do not reconcile them.
- 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season [01:01].
- Injury model: gradient-boosted trees (caption spelling "XG boost") on 2017-18 Premier League data plus a career injury dataset [03:02]; injury durations sampled from a Gaussian distribution fitted to real injury data [03:32].
- Expected points come from an adapted Maher model, which assumes scoring rates follow a Poisson distribution [05:05]; team identity features were replaced with player skill values from a contribution model captioned "VAPE" [05:36].
- Data: StatsBomb event data for the 17/18 and 18/19 Premier League seasons, Transfermarkt for injury history, Capology for salary [09:11].
- Injury model test: 70/30 split with cross-validation (captioned "five-block"), log loss 0.16 [09:11]; Pearson correlation 0.77 with observed 18/19 outcomes [09:42].
- Selection similarity to real coaches: about 76% for the search model, 82% for the greedy model [10:12].
- Brighton: 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least benefited at 7.5% for the ideal eleven [11:14].
- Average across Premier League teams: 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal eleven [11:44].
- Risk multipliers of two and three times; 1.8% more expected points at three times [12:15].
- Salary cost tied to predicted injuries: 22% reduction for Brighton, about 11% on average [13:16].
- Headline: approximately 13% fewer injuries and an 11% reduction in injury-related costs [14:18]. Inference: the 13% matches the ideal-eleven average, not the 4.6% squad figure; the speaker did not say which. The captions may also garble "five-block."

## Methods and frameworks named

- Markov decision process framing of the coach's selection problem, solved approximately with Monte Carlo tree search using an upper-confidence heuristic and progressive broadening [06:37, 07:38, 08:09].
- Simulation assumes the coach picks the most qualified team in the rolled-out season; values are propagated back to the root [08:09].
- Feature attribution with SHAP values for the injury model [04:03].
- Greedy baseline that maximizes expected points for each match only [10:12].
- Salary data used to translate injuries into wages spent on unavailable players [12:46].

## Limits and open questions

- Built only on free and open data; no club medical or GPS training data [13:48]. Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model [17:53].
- Substitutions are not modeled; rest is all or nothing for a full match [13:48].
- Tested on Premier League only; other leagues, women's sports, rugby and American football are future work [14:18, 19:54].
- Results are simulated; no club has used the recommendations, and the Q&A notes a team would have to be convinced to follow it [18:54].
- Speaker's own framing: it is a decision framework, not a medical prediction model [18:54].
- Sample sizes beyond two seasons are not stated. The company affiliation of the presenter (a startup) is an institutional interest.
- Spoken cost figures conflict ($770 million versus nearly $800 million).

## Q&A

- A questioner proposed optimizing only the next several games, like a survivor pool, and re-optimizing as injuries occur [15:49]; the presenter said the model has a setting for how many games ahead to simulate, including a five-game window [16:51].
- Does the model rely on a reliable injury probability from load and history? Yes [17:22].
- How was load estimated from public data? From event counts, with a separate model imputing physical metrics, since tracking data is not open [17:53].
- Is training load included? No; the aim was a framework, and club medical and training data would improve it [18:24, 18:54].
- Other leagues? Not yet; the design allows other event data and women's sports would be interesting [19:54, 20:24].

=== FILE: videos/2025-03-18_sNWvAaLVS1s_have-the-nerds-ruined-basketball-a-conversation-on-competiti/summary.md ===
---
type: video-summary
video_id: sNWvAaLVS1s
title: "SSAC25: Have the Nerds Ruined Basketball? A Conversation on Competitiveness, Three Pointers,"
event: SSAC25 (MIT Sloan Sports Analytics Conference)
speakers: [Alex Co (introducer, caption spelling), Daryl (caption spelling, surname garbled; 76ers basketball operations), Sue Bird, Mike Zarin (caption spelling; Celtics), Evan Wash (caption spelling; NBA league office), Deepak Motra (moderator, caption spelling)]
topics: [basketball, decision-making, competitive-advantage, policy, front-office]
confidence: untested
caption_source: auto
status: draft
---

## Summary

A moderated panel debates whether analytics-driven optimization, especially the rise of three-point shooting, has hurt basketball. One executive argues the three-point value is too large and the league office should adjust design as teams optimize. A league-office panelist says the only test is whether fans like the resulting product and that the league acts when data show harm, citing a transition-foul rule. Others argue play styles remain varied and that media narrative is the bigger problem. The panel also covers how much weight fan input deserves, public data access, rule-change ideas, and AI. It is opinion and debate, with few verifiable figures.

## Key claims

- The shift in shot locations came from avoiding inefficient two-pointers, since a three is worth 50% more [02:03].
- One panelist says the three-point value is too large and the league should step in as teams optimize [03:04, 03:37].
- The league-office panelist says a rule is a problem only if the resulting playstyle is not exciting, and that fans like the three-point era overall [05:09, 05:40].
- A team executive says the claim that all teams play one style is untrue, citing varied styles and open three-point looks [09:47].
- The same side says the spread of play styles between teams is about as wide as before [10:17].
- Fan engagement and a large media deal are cited as evidence the product is healthy [11:18].
- The narrative about the three-point revolution, not the game itself, is described as a problem that shapes fan opinion, and players dislike being told to do the same thing every possession [12:19, 12:49].
- Panelists place low to middling weight on what fans say they want; behavioral data count for more [14:20, 14:50].
- The league office tests fan reaction with lab studies using physiological monitors [15:20].
- Public data access has narrowed: team-held player-pose data are not public, which limits what a young analyst can do [19:57, 20:28].
- A former player says missing WNBA data left gaps in the history and stories of the game [18:55].
- Rules set incentives that push well-run teams in one direction, and whether that direction is better or worse is not known in advance [22:29].
- The league says it has acted where the optimal play hurt the game, for example transition fouls and the draft lottery [24:30, 25:00].
- Most fan rule-change suggestions are easier to voice than to implement because of second-order effects [26:31, 33:34].
- Panelists expect AI to change on-court play less than analytics already has, with bigger effects off the court [37:06, 37:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- 100 most common shooting spots in 2001-2002 shown against about 15 years later [01:32, 02:03].
- Three-pointers worth 50% more than other shots [02:03].
- About 15% of an NBA game is shooting [04:38].
- Over 60% of one team's three-pointers are open [09:47].
- Gap between the lowest and highest three-point-shooting teams: something like 18% in 2012, now 15 or 16 [10:47]. The captions are garbled here; do not rely on it.
- Fan-weight scale of 1 to 10: answers of three, about six or seven, and five [14:20, 14:50]; speaker attribution is unclear in the captions.
- Roughly 1,500 plays a season affected by transition fouls before the rule [24:30].
- WNBA season length: 40 games last season, 44 next season; Sue Bird played 32, 34 and 36 in different stretches [18:24].
- Tracking data described as 29 pose points at 60 frames per second [19:57].
- Hiring exercise: 100 points across analytical ability, interpersonal skills and passion; one answer was 40, 40 and 20 [35:05, 36:06]; other answers are garbled.
- Ten-year prediction question about three-point attempts being 20% higher [38:40]; the captions mix up the numbers (including 42%) and cannot be trusted.

## Methods and frameworks named

- Shot-location maps over time, and a team-level measure of how different play styles are (shooting positions, offensive set mix) [10:17, 10:47].
- Fan research from survey data, minute-by-minute viewing behavior, attendance, lab studies with heart rate and skin temperature monitors, and a planned ethnographic home-viewing study [14:50, 15:20].
- Decision rule from the league: act when data are clear, and consider stakeholder views as a proxy for fans [25:00].
- Informal survey of conference registrants for rule ideas, read aloud [28:31].

## Limits and open questions

- Panel of executives and a former player speaking from institutional positions (league office, teams); no data were shown beyond images and spoken figures, and no sample sizes are given.
- The captions have no speaker labels and several passages are garbled, so some attributions and figures are uncertain.
- The panelists disagree and do not resolve whether the three-point value is too high [03:04, 05:09, 24:00].
- Claims that fan satisfaction did not change during the season rest on the league's own survey and social data, which were not shown [12:19].
- Rapid-fire answers (rule change predictions, AI, hiring weights) were casual.

## Q&A

- Dominant strategy in 5 to 10 years: more players trained from youth to switch, shoot threes and rebound; more physicality if rules stay [40:13, 40:43].
- Whether physicality is at the right level: views differ, with concern it is too physical [41:13, 42:13].
- Defense: panelists say defense has become more skilled and gets too little media attention [43:14].
- Last question to Sue: analytics did not shape her WNBA career much, and she finds playing without thinking about shot value more fun [45:18].

Caption problems: both transcripts are auto captions with garbled passages; in K5a7C4b1Cwc the spoken cost figures ($770 million vs nearly $800 million) conflict and "five-block", "VAPE" and "Maya/Maher" look mis-transcribed; in sNWvAaLVS1s there are no speaker labels, names (Daryl, Mike Zarin, Evan Wash, Deepak Motra) are garbled, and the variance, ten-year prediction and rapid-fire numbers ([10:47], [38:40]) are unreliable.
